lesson.title: The z-star Toolkit: Standard Critical Values for Common Confidence Levels
lesson.summary: A small set of z critical values, 1.645, 1.96, and 2.576, covers the vast majority of confidence intervals seen in practice, and knowing when to use them matters as much as knowing the numbers.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter derived critical values from first principles using the standard normal curve and a normal table. In practice, a small handful of z critical values, called z-star values, come up over and over, and it is worth having them memorized as a toolkit rather than rederiving them every time.

For 90% confidence, z-star equals 1.645. For 95% confidence, z-star equals 1.96, the most commonly used confidence level in published research and news polling. For 99% confidence, z-star equals 2.576, used when a much higher standard of reliability is needed, at the cost of a noticeably wider interval. Each of these comes from finding, on the standard normal curve, the z-score that leaves exactly half of the leftover tail probability in the upper tail, exactly as derived in the last chapter.

One caution belongs here. These z critical values are appropriate for confidence intervals about a proportion, and for confidence intervals about a mean when the population standard deviation sigma is genuinely known, both cases relying on the standard normal distribution as the reference. When sigma is unknown and must be estimated from the sample using s, as is true in most real studies involving means, the extra uncertainty from estimating sigma calls for a slightly wider reference distribution called the t-distribution instead of the normal distribution. That distribution and its own critical values, t-star, are the subject of a later unit. For now, it is enough to know that the clean z-star values in this chapter assume sigma is known.

To see the z critical values generalize beyond the transit survey, consider the bottling plant example again, with known sigma equals 10 milliliters, sample size n equals 50, sample mean x-bar equals 500 milliliters, and standard error approximately 1.4142 milliliters. Building a 90% confidence interval this time instead of a 95% one, the critical value is z-star equals 1.645, so the margin of error is 1.645 times 1.4142, which equals approximately 2.33 milliliters. The 90% confidence interval is 500 minus 2.33 to 500 plus 2.33, or 497.67 to 502.33 milliliters, narrower than the 95% interval of 497.23 to 502.77 milliliters computed earlier, exactly as expected from a lower confidence level's smaller critical value. This is the same z-star toolkit, applied to a fresh scenario, producing the same reliable arithmetic: point estimate, plus or minus, critical value times standard error.
